claims.text: The preserved source explicitly asks for deadlock avoidance demonstrated with Java/pseudocode and includes lock ordering, timeout locks and TryLock, but does not provide a business object model or timeout value.

Java SE 21 ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout, unit) can return false when the waiting time elapses and throws InterruptedException if interrupted while acquiring; unlock must release a lock held by the current thread.

Under the candidate contract of a stable unique total order, opposite caller resource directions are normalized to the same acquisition order and complete without a circular lock acquisition in executable stress validation.
The candidate uses one total timeout budget, returns false when a contended second lock is not acquired, releases the already acquired first lock, and propagates interruption without leaking locks.

findings: The answer directly distinguishes structural global lock ordering from timed failure/rollback rather than claiming TryLock alone guarantees progress.

The only source-derived requirements are deadlock avoidance, Java/pseudocode, lock ordering, timeout and TryLock; business resources and timeout numbers are explicitly candidate contracts, not source facts.
The exact Java 21 candidate compiles and opposing A/B versus B/A callers complete 20000 critical sections through the same global order.
Timed second-lock failure releases the first acquired lock; interruption is propagated and cleanup leaves locks acquirable.
The answer states that timeout/retry does not guarantee fairness or eventual success and calls out livelock/starvation as retry-layer risks.
No personal production incident, metric or project result is fabricated; project content is an explicit mapping checklist.
